Rental income and owner cash: separate interest, principal and capital payments

Build a one-year rental cash ledger, then test how missing rent and a capital project change the amount retained or supplied by the owner.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Separate a one-year rental result from owner cash

Interactive planning lab

Rent actually collected in the year$35,200
Cash after all entered payments and allowance$2,000
Annual owner funding gap$0

One invented rental-year cash ledger covering 100% of the hypothetical property’s receipts and payments, not a tax return or property valuation. Rent is collected only in occupied months; entered operating costs continue for all twelve months. Annual interest and principal are independent statement-style inputs, not a mortgage projection. Capital cash and tax allowance are additional, separate uses of cash. The operating-less-interest subtotal is not taxable income. No depreciation, deduction eligibility, arrears recovery, sale, appreciation, borrowing approval or payment-date funding is calculated.

On this page

  1. Begin with money collected and a defined period
  2. Calculate the operating comparator without calling it taxable income
  3. Subtract principal from cash while keeping its economic meaning visible
  4. Include the capital payment and tax cash once each
  5. Test the rent-collection months and larger cash outlays
  6. Add the calendar before relying on a positive annual total

The central idea

An operating subtotal is different from cash available to the owner. Principal repayments, capital payments and tax cash can create a funding need even when a narrower income measure is positive.

01

Begin with money collected and a defined period

A rental budget can show several different measures: scheduled rent, rent collected, operating income, debt payments and cash retained. Giving each number a separate name prevents one from being used as a substitute for another.

The default example covers one year and all of the modeled property’s receipts and payments. Rent is CAD 3,200 for each occupied month, with one whole month producing no rent. Collected rent is therefore 11 × CAD 3,200 = CAD 35,200. There is no assumed later recovery of the missing month’s rent.

The no-rent-month input is a cash stress, not a local vacancy statistic or an assessment of a tenancy. It can represent a deliberately simplified collection gap, but it does not decide contractual rent owed, legal remedies or the treatment of a bad debt. A real ledger needs the actual receipts and the period to which they relate.

02

Calculate the operating comparator without calling it taxable income

Operating cash costs are assumed to continue at CAD 600 for every month, including the month without collected rent. Their annual total is CAD 7,200. The model also includes CAD 10,000 of independently entered annual loan interest.

Collected rent less those operating costs and interest is CAD 18,000. This is the article’s explicitly limited operating-less-interest comparator. It is not a tax assessment or a complete accounting profit, and it includes no depreciation, capital cost allowance, accrual adjustment or review of deduction eligibility.

The CRA’s rental-expense guidance distinguishes current and capital expenses and sets out conditions for deductions. A cash payment’s label alone does not establish its tax treatment. These charts accept independently supported cash inputs and preserve the distinction between a teaching subtotal and an actual rental-income calculation.

03

Subtract principal from cash while keeping its economic meaning visible

The owner pays another CAD 8,000 toward loan principal during the year. That payment uses cash and reduces a liability. It is separate from the CAD 10,000 interest cost, even if both appear inside the same regular mortgage debit.

The CRA states that rental-property mortgage or loan principal repayments are not deductible. This is one reason a tax-oriented income number and an owner’s cash flow can differ. The model does not assume that a principal payment becomes a freely available asset that can pay the next bill.

Annual principal and interest are entered separately. The tool does not infer them from the total mortgage payment, calculate an amortization schedule or project a future renewal rate. Use a supported statement breakdown when replacing the example. Counting the whole mortgage debit as interest would misdescribe both this cash ledger and the underlying repayment.

04

Include the capital payment and tax cash once each

The example pays CAD 5,000 for a separate capital project and allocates CAD 3,000 to tax cash. Both amounts sit outside the CAD 600 monthly operating-cost entry. The default reconciliation is CAD 18,000 − CAD 8,000 − CAD 5,000 − CAD 3,000 = CAD 2,000 retained cash.

The capital input is a payment, rather than an estimate of how much market value the project creates. A CAD 5,000 outlay does not automatically increase the property’s sale price by CAD 5,000. The calculator also makes no deduction or depreciation claim for it.

The tax allowance is independently entered. It is not a percentage automatically applied to the operating subtotal, a final tax bill or a refund calculation. A tax payment or earmark can reflect other facts and dates. Keep the amount outside operating costs if it is entered here, and avoid including the same cash use in two fields.

05

Test the rent-collection months and larger cash outlays

The line chart changes the number of months with collected rent while retaining all annual payments. Its two lines differ by principal repayments, capital cash and the tax allowance. Their vertical separation explains how the same receipt pattern can produce a positive operating comparator and a much smaller owner cash result.

With the default payments, annual cash uses total CAD 33,200. At CAD 3,200 per collected month, the arithmetic threshold is 10.375 months. Because the control uses whole months, eleven collected months produce positive annual cash and ten produce a CAD 1,200 annual funding gap.

The matrix combines no-rent months with alternative capital cash payments. It assigns no likelihood to either stress. A negative cell records money the owner would need to supply over the year; it does not authorize borrowing, identify an available credit line or show the maximum balance that could be needed between actual receipt and payment dates.

06

Add the calendar before relying on a positive annual total

A one-year surplus does not establish that an early bill is funded. A large repair payment can arrive before later rent, while property taxes or insurance may be payable on particular dates. Put those dates beside accessible opening cash to measure the actual short-term buffer.

This model excludes the initial purchase, down payment, land-transfer costs, selling costs, changes in property value and return on the owner’s invested capital. It therefore does not calculate a property investment return or establish whether purchasing a rental is attractive. It also excludes shared ownership, personal-use portions and short-term-rental-specific rules.

Use the ledger to reconcile supported receipts with distinct cash uses, then obtain the accounting and tax calculations appropriate to the actual property. The planning output is the amount retained or supplied under the entered year’s assumptions, with the economic role of each payment visible. It is a starting point for a dated cash plan rather than a substitute for one.
